'''John Hamilton Bowie''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|sep=,|AM}} (born 16 July 1938<ref name="encyclopedia">{{cite book |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780081003794/the-encyclopedia-of-mass-spectrometry |title=The Encyclopedia of Mass Spectrometry |isbn=9780081003794 |format= |accessdate= |last1=Nier |first1=Keith A. |last2=Yergey |first2=Alfred L. |last3=Jane Gale |first3=P. |date=6 May 2015 |publisher=Elsevier Science }}</ref>) is an Australian scientist and academic,<ref>{{Citation |last=Downard |first=Kevin M. |title=John Hamilton Bowie |date=2015-01-01 |work=The Encyclopedia of Mass Spectrometry |pages=25–26 |editor-last=Gross |editor-first=Michael L. |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780081003794000599 |access-date=2026-09-30 |place=Boston |publisher=Elsevier |doi=10.1016/B978-0-08-100379-4.00059-9 |isbn=978-0-08-100379-4 |editor2-last=Caprioli |editor2-first=Richard M.|url-access=subscription }}</ref> best known for his contributions to research in the fields of the chemistry of negative ions in the gas phase and of bio-active [[peptide]]s in skin glands.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.anzsms.org/History/bowie.pdf |title=Richard A. J. O'Hair, "John Hamilton Bowie: an appreciation", ''Australian Journal of Chemistry'' 2003, 56, pp 343-348 |access-date=1 August 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160406020553/http://www.anzsms.org/History/bowie.pdf |archive-date=6 April 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career and Research==
Bowie was born as the only child of William Hamilton Bowie and Alice Maud Bowie (nee Boyce), educated in Melbourne,<ref>[http://www.eoas.info/biogs/P000973b.htm ''Encyclopedia of Australian Science''- Biographical Entry ]</ref> and graduated from the [[University of Melbourne]] where he obtained an MSc for his work on the colouring matters of Australian plants. In 1961 he started working with [[Alan Woodworth Johnson|Alan Johnson]] obtained his PhD at the [[University of Nottingham]] on the structures of various antibiotics including streptolidine, viomycin, and rhodomycinone, where he came across mass spectrometry for the first time.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He subsequently took up an ICI postdoctoral fellowship at the [[University of Cambridge]] under [[Alexander R. Todd, Baron Todd|Lord Todd]]. 

In 1966, he was appointed to a lectureship at the [[University of Adelaide]], rising to become head of department.  In 1968 he was awarded the [[Rennie Memorial Medal]] for his work on the rearrangement of positively charged organic molecules.{{citation needed|date=June 2025}}  In 1974 he was awarded the H. G. Smith Memorial Medal of the [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]] and in 2001 the A.J. Birch medal. In 2006 he received the Thomson Medal.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> From 1989 to 1992 he was Pro-Vice-Chancellor of the university.

In 2017, Bowie was appointed a [[Order of Australia|Member of the Order of Australia]] for significant service to science in the field of mass spectrometry, and to education as an academic, researcher and author.<ref name=AM.gen.div.A-L>{{cite web |url=http://www.gg.gov.au/sites/default/files/files/honours/ad/ad2017/slkh83xzcb/AM%20Final%20Media%20Notes%20(A-L)2.pdf |title=Member (AM) in the General Division of the Order of Australia (A-L) |work=2017 Australia Day Honours List |publisher=[[Governor-General of Australia|Office of the Governor-General of Australia]] |date=26 January 2017 |accessdate=26 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190321173101/http://www.gg.gov.au/sites/default/files/files/honours/ad/ad2017/slkh83xzcb/AM%20Final%20Media%20Notes%20(A-L)2.pdf |archive-date=21 March 2019 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
